lessons.title: Immediate Family Members
lessons.body: In Shona culture, family is the cornerstone of society. Immediate family members include father, mother, siblings, and children. Start by learning the core terms: baba (father), amai (mother), mukoma (older brother), munin'ina (younger sibling), hanzvadzi (sister for a male speaker), and mwarikadzi (sister for a female speaker). For children: mwanakomana (son) and mwanasikana (daughter). Practice by introducing your own family: "Uyu ndi baba vangu" (This is my father). Use real photos on your phone to label each person. In rural areas, extended family often lives nearby, but immediate family remains the primary unit. In urban settings like Harare or Bulawayo, nuclear families are common, but ties to rural home remain strong. When greeting, show respect: "Mangwanani baba" (Good morning father). For siblings, use age relative terms: mukoma for older brother, and for older sister, use hanzvadzi (if you are male) or mwarikadzi (if you are female). Younger siblings are munin'ina regardless of gender. Practice with a friend: ask "Une vana vangani?" (How many children do you have?) and respond "Ndine vana vaviri" (I have two children). Numbers: poshi (one), piri (two), tatu (three). Use these in sentences: "Ndine vana vatatu" (I have three children). Remember that Shona uses different terms for maternal and paternal relatives, which we'll cover in the next lesson. For now, master these basics by writing them down and saying them aloud daily. Create flashcards with the English on one side and Shona on the other. Test yourself: What is the Shona word for mother? (Amai). Father? (Baba). Sister (to a male)? (Hanzvadzi). Spend 10 minutes each day reviewing. Then, introduce your family to a Shona speaker. Ask them to correct your pronunciation. Shona is a tonal language, so pay attention to pitch: baba (father) has low-high tone, while baba (grandfather) is different. But for immediate family, context usually clarifies. Practice with common phrases: "Ndine hanzvadzi imwe" (I have one sister). "Mukoma wangu anogara muHarare" (My older brother lives in Harare). This lesson gives you the foundation to talk about your closest relatives.

lessons.title: Extended Family Terms
lessons.body: Shona extended family terms are rich and reflect the importance of kinship. Your father's brothers are all called babamukuru (older) or babamunini (younger), and their wives are maiguru or mainini. Your mother's sisters are all amai, with their husbands called babamukuru or babamunini depending on age relative to your mother. For your father's sister, use tete; her husband is sekuru. Your mother's brother is mwaramu or sekuru, and his wife is maiguru or mainini. Grandparents: mbuya (grandmother) and sekuru (grandfather). Great-grandparents: tateguru (great-grandfather) and tateguru (great-grandmother). Cousins: hama (cousins from father's side) and muzukuru (cousins from mother's side, or nephew/niece). In-laws: father-in-law is tezvara, mother-in-law is vamwene, son-in-law is mukwasha, daughter-in-law is muroora. These terms are used in daily life. For example, when you visit your rural home, you greet your tete with "Mangwanani tete" and she may respond "Mangwanani mwanangu" (Good morning my child). Use these terms to show respect. In Shona culture, calling someone by the correct kinship term is more polite than using their name. Practice by drawing a family tree. Label each person with the correct Shona term. For example, your mother's older sister is amai (or specifically maiguru if older than your mother). Your father's younger brother is babamunini. Use real examples: "Tete vangu vanogara muMutare" (My aunt lives in Mutare). "Sekuru vangu ndivo vakandidzidzisa kurima" (My grandfather taught me farming). Note that some terms depend on the speaker's gender. For instance, a man calls his sister's children muzukuru, while a woman calls her brother's children muzukuru as well. But a man's sister is hanzvadzi, and a woman's sister is mwarikadzi. This complexity shows the importance of relationships. To practice, ask a Shona speaker about their family: "Une tete here?" (Do you have an aunt?). Listen to how they use the terms. Then, try to describe your own extended family. Write 5 sentences using at least 5 different extended family terms. Review daily. In no time, you'll navigate Shona family gatherings with confidence.

lessons.title: Describing Relationships
lessons.body: Describing relationships in Shona involves using verbs and adjectives to explain how people are connected. Start with basic verbs: kuva (to be), kuva ne (to have), kuda (to love), kubatsira (to help), kuchengeta (to take care of). For example, "Ndine hanzvadzi" (I have a sister). "Mukoma wangu anondida" (My older brother loves me). "Amai vanochengeta mhuri" (Mother takes care of the family). To describe relationship quality, use adjectives: hukama hwakanaka (good relationship), hukama hwakaipa (bad relationship), hukama hwepedyo (close relationship), hukama hwokure (distant relationship). For example: "Ndine hukama hwakanaka na tete vangu" (I have a good relationship with my aunt). "Hukama hwedu hwakaoma" (Our relationship is difficult). You can also use verbs like kuwirirana (to get along), kusawirirana (to not get along), kuvimbana (to trust each other). "Tinowirirana nemurume wangu" (I get along with my husband). "Hanzvadzi dzangu hadziwirirane" (My sisters don't get along). To ask about relationships: "Une hukama sei na...?" (What is your relationship with...?). "Munowirirana here?" (Do you get along?). Practice by describing your own relationships. For instance: "Ndine hukama hwepedyo na amai vangu. Tinotaurirana mazuva ose. Vanondibatsira nezvidzidzo.

Nguva dzose tinodya pamwe chete" (We always eat together). "Kashoma kunetsana" (We rarely argue). Also, learn to describe family roles: baba ndiye musoro wemburi (father is the head of the family), amai ndivo moyo wemburi (mother is the heart of the family). In urban areas, these roles may shift, but the language remains. To practice, write a short paragraph describing your family relationships. Use at least 5 different verbs and 3 adjectives. Then, record yourself saying it. Listen for pronunciation. Share with a Shona speaker for feedback. This will build your confidence in talking about relationships.

lessons.title: Possessive Pronouns for Family
lessons.body: Possessive pronouns in Shona are essential for talking about family. They change based on the noun class of the possessed item. For family members, most belong to different noun classes. For example, 'mother' (amai) is in class 2 (plural), so 'my mother' is amai vangu. 'Father' (baba) is also class 2, so baba vangu. 'Older brother' (mukoma) is class 1, so mukoma wangu. 'Younger sibling' (munin'ina) is class 1, so munin'ina wangu. 'Sister' (hanzvadzi) is class 9, so hanzvadzi yangu. 'Child' (mwana) is class 1, so mwana wangu. 'Children' (vana) is class 2, so vana vangu. 'Husband' (murume) is class 1, so murume wangu. 'Wife' (mukadzi) is class 1, so mukadzi wangu. Learn the pattern: class 1 uses wangu, class 2 uses vangu, class 9 uses yangu, class 4 (plural of class 3) uses yangu, etc. But for family, focus on these common ones. Practice with sentences: "Amai vangu vanogara muKadoma" (My mother lives in Kadoma). "Baba vangu vanoshanda kumigodhi" (My father works at the mines). "Mukoma wangu anodzidza kuyunivhesiti" (My older brother studies at university). "Hanzvadzi yangu ine mwana" (My sister has a child). "Vana vangu vanoenda kuchikoro" (My children go to school). To ask 'whose?', use ndiani? For example: "Ndiani amai vako?" (Who is your mother?). Respond: "Amai vangu ndiMary" (My mother is Mary). Note that vako is used for class 2 (your), wako for class 1, yako for class 9. For example: "Baba vako ndiani?" (Who is your father?). "Mukoma wako anoshanda kupi?" (Where does your older brother work?). Practice by creating a family tree and labeling each person with the correct possessive. For example: "Baba vangu" (my father), "Amai vangu" (my mother), "Mukoma wangu" (my older brother), "Munin'ina wangu" (my younger sibling), "Hanzvadzi yangu" (my sister). Then, introduce your family to someone: "Uyu ndi baba vangu. Uyu ndi amai vangu. Uyu ndi mukoma wangu." Do this daily until it becomes automatic. Also, learn to use possessives with extended family: "Tete vangu" (my aunt), "Sekuru vangu" (my grandfather), "Mbuya vangu" (my grandmother). Notice that many use vangu because they are class 2 (respectful plural). This is a key cultural point: elders are often referred to in plural to show respect.

lessons.title: Talking About Marital Status
lessons.body: Talking about marital status in Shona is straightforward. Common terms: kuroora (for a man to marry), kukwira (for a woman to marry), kuroorwa (to be married, for a woman). To ask someone's marital status: "Wakaroora here?" (Are you married? - to a man). "Wakakwira here?" (Are you married? - to a woman). Or more generally: "Une murume here?" (Do you have a husband?) "Une mukadzi here?" (Do you have a wife?). Responses: "Hongu, ndakaroora" (Yes, I am married - man). "Hongu, ndakakwira" (Yes, I am married - woman). "Aiwa, handisati ndaroora" (No, I am not yet married - man). "Aiwa, handisati ndakwira" (No, I am not yet married - woman). "Ndakarambwa" (I am divorced - man). "Ndakarambwa" (I am divorced - woman). "Ndine chirikadzi" (I am a widow). "Ndine murume akafa" (I am a widower). "Ndine musikana" (I have a girlfriend). "Ndine mukomana" (I have a boyfriend). In Shona culture, marriage is a significant milestone, often arranged with lobola (bride price). To talk about engagement: "Takavimbisana" (We are engaged). "Tave muchirango" (We are in a relationship). Practice by asking and answering these questions. For example: "Wakaroora here?" "Hongu, ndakaroora. Ndine mukadzi nemwana." (Yes, I am married. I have a wife and child.) "Une vana vangani?" (How many children do you have?) "Ndine vana vaviri" (I have two children). To talk about future plans: "Ndicharoora gore rinouya" (I will marry next year). "Ndichakwira mushure mekupedza chikoro" (I will marry after finishing school). Note that in urban areas, many young people use "Ndine mudikani" (I have a partner) which is more informal. Also, learn to ask about someone else's marital status politely: "Murume wako ndiani?" (Who is your husband?) "Mukadzi wako anoshanda kupi?" (Where does your wife work?). For divorced: "Vakarambana" (They divorced). For separated: "Vakaparadzana" (They separated). Practice with a friend: role-play a conversation where you ask about marital status and respond. Use real numbers: "Ndine vana vatatu" (I have three children). "Ndakaroora makore gumi" (I have been married for ten years). This lesson gives you the vocabulary to discuss marital status confidently.

lessons.title: Family Traditions and Roles
lessons.body: Shona family traditions and roles are deeply rooted in culture. Traditionally, the father (baba) is the head of the family, responsible for providing and making major decisions. The mother (amai) manages the household, cares for children, and often handles finances. In rural areas, children have roles: boys herd cattle (kufudza mombe) and help with farming, while girls help with cooking (kubika) and cleaning (kutsvaira). In urban settings, these roles are more flexible, but respect for elders remains paramount. Key traditions include: kurova guva (ceremony to bring back the spirit of a deceased family member), roora/lobola (bride price negotiation), and kugadzira (family gatherings). During lobola, the groom's family brings goods or money to the bride's family. For example, in 2023, typical lobola in Zimbabwe ranges from US$2,000 to US$10,000 depending on the family. The process involves uncles and aunts (sekuru na tete) as negotiators. Another tradition is kusungira (tying the knot) which is a small ceremony before the big wedding. Family roles also include the eldest son (dangwe) who often becomes the heir. The eldest daughter (dangwe) helps raise younger siblings. Respect is shown through language: children kneel (kupfugama) when greeting elders, especially in rural areas. Use phrases: "Mangwanani baba, ndapfugama" (Good morning father, I kneel). "Mhoroi amai" (Hello mother). During family gatherings, the order of speaking is important: elders speak first, then others. To participate, listen and wait for your turn. Practice by attending a family event if possible. Ask your elders about traditions: "Tsanangurai tsika dzedu" (Explain our traditions). Learn proverbs: "Musha mukadzi" (The home is a woman) emphasizing the mother's role. "Rume rimwe harikombi churu" (One man cannot surround an anthill) meaning teamwork. To integrate, help with chores: "Ndichabatsira kubika" (I will help cook). "Ndichafudza mombe" (I will herd cattle). In urban areas, families may not have cattle, but helping with shopping or cleaning is valued. This lesson helps you understand and participate in Shona family life respectfully.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Shona Family & Relationship Terms for Agri-Business

In Zimbabwe's agribusiness sector, relationships are the infrastructure of commerce. Whether you are negotiating a maize supply contract in Mashonaland, onboarding seasonal tobacco labourers in Manicaland, or structuring a family-run poultry operation in Masvingo, your ability to speak about family in Shona signals respect, trustworthiness, and cultural fluency. This Practical Reference lesson consolidates the vocabulary, grammar, and cultural protocols from the six core lessons into a single working document you can use in the field, at the market, and in the boardroom.

Shona family terminology is not merely social language â it is operational language. Land inheritance, labour mobilisation, savings groups (mukando), and informal credit all flow through kinship networks. Knowing who is sekuru (maternal uncle) versus babamukuru (paternal uncle) can determine who holds decision-making authority over a shared irrigation scheme. This lesson is built for business-first application.

Table 1: Immediate Family Terms with Business Usage

Shona Term English Meaning Agribusiness Context
BabaFatherOften the land title holder; approval needed for lease agreements.
AmaiMotherManages household food security and often the poultry/vegetable micro-enterprise.
MukomaOlder siblingFrequently the co-signatory on cooperative loans.
Munin'inaYounger siblingLabour mobilisation for planting and harvesting seasons.
MwanakomanaSonSuccession planning for the family farm or transport business.
MwanasikanaDaughterIncreasingly lead operators of agro-processing SMEs.
Mudzimai / MukadziWifeJoint decision-maker in household agri-investment.
MurumeHusbandCustomary authority in cattle transactions.

Source: Compiled from Chimhundu, H. (2002) Dura Mazwi: ShonaâEnglish Dictionary (College Press, Harare) and the ALLEX Project corpus, University of Zimbabwe.

Table 2: Extended Family & Relationship Terms

Shona Term English Meaning Business Relevance
SekuruGrandfather / maternal uncleCustomary mediator in land disputes and inheritance.
MbuyaGrandmotherKeeper of family history and traditional seed knowledge.
TeteAunt (father's sister)Advisor in marriage negotiations affecting business alliances.
BabamukuruFather's elder brotherSenior authority in patrilineal clan decisions.
MuzukuruNephew / niece / grandchildTrusted junior staff in family-run operations.
MurooraDaughter-in-lawOften integrated into family enterprise labour force.
MukwashaSon-in-lawMay bring external capital or labour into the household.
HamaRelative / kinBroad network used for savings groups (mukando).
MhuriFamilyBasic unit of agricultural production in communal areas.

Source: Adapted from Bourdillon, M.F.C. (1976) The Shona Peoples (Mambo Press, Gweru) and Shona teaching resources from the University of Zimbabwe.

â  SAFETY & CULTURAL WARNING

Never assume a Shona business contact's family structure based on Western norms. Using the wrong kinship term â for example, calling a tete (paternal aunt) an amai (mother), or addressing a mukoma as a munin'ina â can cause serious offence and damage commercial trust. When in doubt, use the respectful generic hama (relative) or ask a trusted local intermediary. In rural land negotiations, always identify and greet the senior sekuru or babamukuru first; bypassing them can void informal agreements and expose your business to community-level reputational risk.

Grammar Quick Note: Possessive Pronouns for Family

Shona possessive pronouns agree with the noun class of the possessed item. For family terms, most belong to class 1 (singular) or class 2 (plural). Business-critical examples:

  • Baba vangu â my father
  • Amai vangu â my mother
  • Mukoma wangu â my older sibling
  • Hama dzedu â our relatives
  • Mhuri yedu â our family
  • Mudzimai wangu â my wife
  • Murume wangu â my husband

Note the respectful plural vangu for parents and elders â a grammatical marker of deference that also functions as a business courtesy when addressing senior partners.

Talking About Marital Status in Business Contexts

Shona uses direct but polite constructions. Useful for onboarding forms, cooperative registers, and community meetings:

  • Ndakatora / Ndaroora â I am married (male / female speaker)
  • Handina kuroora / Handina kuroorwa â I am not married
  • Ndakarambana â I am divorced
  • Mudzimai wangu akafa â My wife has died (widower)
  • Murume wangu akafa â My husband has died (widow)

In agribusiness, marital status often determines access to land, credit, and cooperative membership. Recording it accurately â and respectfully â is both a legal and cultural necessity.

Family Traditions and Roles in Agri-Enterprise

Traditional Shona family roles map directly onto agricultural value chains. The baba typically controls cattle and land title; the amai manages seed banks, poultry, and vegetable gardens; mukoma and munin'ina provide seasonal labour; tete and sekuru arbitrate disputes and bless major transactions. Understanding these roles allows agribusiness operators to negotiate with the right decision-maker the first time, reducing transaction costs and building long-term community goodwill.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Greet the senior male (sekuru / babamukuru) first in rural negotiations.
  2. Use vangu (respectful plural) when referring to parents and elders.
  3. Confirm marital status before drafting land or credit agreements.
  4. Identify the amai's role in household food and micro-enterprise operations.
  5. Never misclassify tete vs amai â kinship precision equals commercial credibility.
  6. Map the hama network before launching a mukando or savings scheme.
  7. Record mhuri (family) structure for cooperative registration accuracy.
  8. Ask a trusted local intermediary when unsure of a kinship term.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • University of Zimbabwe â Department of African Languages and Literature (open teaching resources on Shona grammar and kinship).
  • ALLEX Project â African Languages Lexical Corpus (ShonaâEnglish dictionary data).
  • FAO Zimbabwe (agribusiness and rural household resources).
  • ZIMSTAT â Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency (household and agricultural survey data).
  • Ministry of Lands, Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Rural Development (Zimbabwe).

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'father'?
quiz.explanation: Baba means father in Shona.

quiz.q: How do you say 'my mother' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: Amai vangu means my mother, using the correct possessive for class 2.

quiz.q: What is the term for 'older brother'?
quiz.explanation: Mukoma is used for older brother.

quiz.q: Which word means 'sister' when spoken by a male?
quiz.explanation: A male speaker uses hanzvadzi for sister.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'children'?
quiz.explanation: Vana is the plural for children.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I have two children'?
quiz.explanation: Vaviri means two, so 'Ndine vana vaviri' is correct.

quiz.q: What is the term for 'grandmother'?
quiz.explanation: Mbuya means grandmother.

quiz.q: Which term refers to your father's sister?
quiz.explanation: Tete is your father's sister.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'father-in-law'?
quiz.explanation: Tezvara means father-in-law.

quiz.q: How do you say 'my aunt' (father's sister)?
quiz.explanation: Tete vangu means my aunt (father's sister).

quiz.q: What does 'hukama hwakanaka' mean?
quiz.explanation: Hukama hwakanaka means good relationship.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Do you get along?' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: Munowirirana here? means 'Do you get along?'

quiz.q: Which verb means 'to love'?
quiz.explanation: Kuda means to love.

quiz.q: What is the possessive for 'my' with class 1 nouns (e.g., mukoma)?
quiz.explanation: Class 1 nouns take wangu, e.g., mukoma wangu.

quiz.q: How do you say 'my sister' (for a male speaker)?
quiz.explanation: Hanzvadzi yangu is correct for a male speaker's sister.

quiz.q: What is the possessive for 'your' with class 2 nouns (e.g., baba)?
quiz.explanation: Class 2 nouns take vako, e.g., baba vako.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Are you married?' to a man?
quiz.explanation: Wakaroora here? is used for a man.

quiz.q: What does 'ndakarambwa' mean?
quiz.explanation: Ndakarambwa means I am divorced.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am not yet married' (for a woman)?
quiz.explanation: Handisati ndakwira is used by a woman.

quiz.q: What is the term for 'bride price'?
quiz.explanation: Roora is the Shona term for bride price, also known as lobola.

quiz.q: Who is traditionally the head of the family?
quiz.explanation: Baba (father) is traditionally the head.

quiz.q: What is the ceremony to bring back a deceased's spirit?
quiz.explanation: Kurova guva is the ceremony to bring back the spirit.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I will help cook'?
quiz.explanation: Ndichabatsira kubika means I will help cook.

quiz.q: What does 'Musha mukadzi' mean?
options: A) The home is a woman
B) The home is a man
C) The home is a child
D) The home is a family
quiz.explanation: Musha mukadzi is a proverb meaning the home is a woman.

quiz.q: Which term means 'eldest son'?
quiz.explanation: Dangwe refers to the eldest son.

quiz.q: How do you show respect when greeting an elder?
quiz.explanation: Kupfugama means to kneel, a sign of respect.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'husband'?
quiz.explanation: Murume means husband.

quiz.q: How do you say 'my wife'?
quiz.explanation: Mukadzi wangu means my wife.

quiz.q: What is the term for 'cousin' from mother's side?
quiz.explanation: Muzukuru is used for cousins from the mother's side.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'How many children do you have?'
quiz.explanation: Une vana vangani? means 'How many children do you have?'
